title: EncroChat
text:
The EncroChat encrypted messaging service and the related customised phones were discovered by France's National Gendarmerie in 2017 when conducting operations against organised crime gangs.[1,2] At the time of the Fellows and Boyle trial in December 2018, the NCA struggled to crack the lock screen passcode, as anything was wiped out after a set number of attempts.[3,4]

The investigation accelerated in early 2019 after receiving EU funding.[1] At the end of January 2020, a judge in Lille, France, authorised the infiltration of the EncroChat servers.[5] Intelligence and technical collaboration between the NCA, the National Gendarmerie and Dutch police culminated in gaining access to messages after the National Gendarmerie put a "technical tool" on EncroChat's servers in France.[6,2,7] The malware allowed them to read messages before they were sent and record lock screen passwords. Messages could be read by law enforcement beginning in April.[8] EncroChat estimated that around 50% of devices in Europe were affected in June 2020.[7,9]

The National Gendarmerie formed a special unit to investigate the hacked information on 15 March 2020, then signed an agreement with the Dutch Police to form a joint investigation team (JIT) on 10 April, co-operating through Eurojust with the support of Europol.[1] The data was distributed by the JIT to other European partners, including the UK, Sweden and Norway.[10] The NCA began to receive information about the content of messages on 1 April 2020,[1] then started to build data analysis technology to automatically "identify and locate offenders by analysing millions of messages and hundreds of thousands of images".[11] The chief of the Dutch National Police Force, , compared the malware to "sitting at the table where criminals were chatting among themselves".[12] In May 2020, the wipe feature was disabled at distance by law enforcement in some units. The company initially tried to push an update in response to what was initially regarded as a bug, but the devices were struck again by malware altering lock screen passwords.[7,9]

On the night of 12–13 June 2020, once EncroChat suspected the infiltration by law enforcement had occurred,[1] users received a secret message:

> Today, we had our domain seized illegally by government entities(s). They repurposed our domain to launch an attack to compromise the carbon units. ... Due to the level of sophistication of the attack and the malware code, we can no longer guarantee the security of your device. ... You are advises [sic] to power off and physically dispose your device immediately.[7,9]

A few days later, an "email address long associated with EncroChat" informed Vice Motherboard that the service was shutting down permanently "following several attacks carried out by a foreign organisation that seems to originate in the UK"; Cox publicly disclosed excerpts of the email on 22 June.[13] Europol and the National Crime Agency refused to comment at the time.[7] The identity of the persons in charge of EncroChat has not been revealed as of 3 July 2020.[14]
